###### Abstract
A powerful data structure for causal inference is staggered adoption: many units are observed over many time periods, during which some units adopt an irreversible treatment at various time points while others remain untreated. Popular methods that apply in this setting include difference in difference, fixed effects, matching, and synthetic control. All of these methods compare the future outcomes of treatment adopters and non-adopters to answer the question: for units who adopt treatment, what outcomes would have been realized if they had remained untreated? We show that this question actually hides two very different causal questions of interest.

## 10.1 Why TWFE fails with staggered adoption
#### The “forbidden comparisons”
The DiD logic from the previous chapter compares the treated group’s change with the change in a clean, untreated control group. In a staggered rollout, TWFE instead uses every available source of variation, including comparisons with already-treated units. This is why TWFE is described as “variation hungry”: some of those extra comparisons use invalid controls.
When treatment effects are the same for all units and constant over time (homogeneous effects), this isn’t a disaster. The bad comparisons wash out, and the TWFE estimate is still a valid, albeit complex, weighted average of the treatment effect. But if treatment effects are heterogeneous — meaning they differ across cohorts or change as units are exposed to the treatment for longer — these forbidden comparisons can introduce bias.

As studies of large-scale healthcare outcomes go, the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment was always slated to be a blockbuster: it’s the only time that researchers have managed to approximate a large, randomized, controlled trial on the effects of giving uninsured people coverage. exa.snippet:
The traditional reason that a researcher runs an experiment is to address selection into treatment. A researcher might be worried that individuals with better outcomes regardless of treatment are more likely to select into treatment, so the simple comparison of treated to untreated individuals will reflect a selection effect as well as a treatment effect. ## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7946162/)Abstract

Nudges influence behavior by changing the environment in which decisions are made, without restricting the menu of options and without altering financial incentives. This paper assesses past empirical research on nudging and provides recommendations for future work in this area by discussing examples of successful and unsuccessful nudges and by analyzing 174 articles that estimate nudge treatment effects. Researchers in disciplines spanning the behavioral sciences, using varied data sources, have documented that many different types of nudges succeed in changing behavior in a wide range of domains. Nudges that automate some aspect of the decision-making process have an average effect size, measured by Cohen’s _d_, that is 0.193 larger than that of other nudges. Our analyses point to the need for future research to pay greater attention to (1) determining which types of nudges tend to be most impactful; (2) using field and laboratory research approaches as complementary methods; (3) measuring long-run effects of nudges; (4) considering effects of nudges on non-targeted outcomes; and (5) examining interaction effects among nudges and other interventions.

The term ‘treatment effect’ refers to the causal effect of a binary (0–1) variable on an outcome variable of scientific or policy interest. Economics examples include the effects of government programmes and policies, such as those that subsidize training for disadvantaged workers, and the effects of individual choices like college attendance. The principal econometric problem in the estimation of treatment effects is selection bias, which arises from the fact that treated individuals differ from the non-treated for reasons other than treatment status per se. Treatment effects can be estimated using social experiments, regression models, matching estimators, and instrumental variables. 

A ‘treatment effect’ is the average causal effect of a binary (0–1) variable on an outcome variable of scientific or policy interest. The term ‘treatment effect’ originates in a medical literature concerned with the causal effects of binary, yes-or-no ‘treatments’, such as an experimental drug or a new surgical procedure. jina.title: What is nudge theory and does it work?
jina.snippet:
*   'Nudges' are techniques used by many entities, including governments, designed to help people make better decisions.

*   New research suggests they are ineffective, and that studies may show positive bias given the widespread investment in such techniques.

*   A better way forward would be to focus on building an evidence base showing which combinations of nudges and other approaches work well together, researchers say.

At the end of last year (2021), there was lots of excitement [about the first comprehensive analysis of past research](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2107346118) on techniques designed to change people’s behaviour (known as “nudging”), confidently showing that they work. This was great news for researchers, but also for governments across the world who have invested in “nudge units” that use such methods.

Nudges [aim to influence people](https://theconversation.com/nudges-four-reasons-to-doubt-popular-technique-to-shape-peoples-behaviour-174359) to make better decisions. For example, authorities may set a “better” choice, such as donating your organs, as a default. Or they could make a healthy food option more attractive through labelling.

But new research reviewing this paper – which had looked at at 212 published papers involving more than 2 million participants – and others now warns nudges may not have any effect on behaviour at all.

To understand why, we need to go into some details about statistics, and how experimental findings are analysed and interpreted. Researchers start off with a hypothesis that there is no effect (null hypothesis). They then ask, what is the probability of getting an actual effect by chance?

So, if in my experiment there is a group of people who are exposed to a specific nudge technique, and a control group that isn’t nudged, my starting point is that the two groups won’t differ. If I then find a difference, I use statistics to work out how probable it is that this would have happened by chance alone.

Unlike traditional interventions aiming to improve people’s behavior, a nudge is low-cost, non-coercive, and less likely to have unintended consequences. More than a decade later, though, nudge enthusiasts readily admit that designing an effective nudge isn’t easy.

For one thing, nudges often are aimed at people who are difficult to engage: those living with hardships like poverty, disability, or limited English proficiency. The stress associated with socioeconomic disadvantages can complicate their efforts to make positive choices and plan for the long term, so nudges that create an encouraging “choice architecture” are welcome. The global COVID-19 pandemic has created significant financial and operational challenges for some businesses. keenable.title: Evaluating Threshold Policies in Randomized Threshold Designs: A Cautionary Tale for Regression Discontinuity Designs
keenable.snippet: Many policies assign treatment according to whether a score crosses a cutoff. Regression discontinuity (RD) designs identify the effect of treatment assignment, but the threshold policy itself may also reshape individuals’ incentives, inducing behavioral responses that affect outcomes even holding treatment status fixed—a channel that conventional RD designs cannot capture. We develop a framework that exploits randomized variation in policy thresholds, together with rank-invariance-type restrictions, to identify the treatment-assignment and incentive-response effects. We illustrate the empirical relevance of this distinction using data from a merit-based scholarship experiment in Malawi. In this illustration, the conventional RD estimate is positive, while the incentive-response effect is negative and more than twice as large in magnitude. These findings suggest that threshold policies may generate unintended adverse behavioral responses, potentially reflecting discouragement induced by demanding thresholds, and caution against relying solely on conventional RD estimates when evaluating threshold policies.

keenable.title: Treatment Effects in the Regression Discontinuity Model with Counterfactual Cutoff and Distorted Running Variables
keenable.snippet:
We develop a new framework for evaluating the total policy effect in regression discontinuity designs (RDD), incorporating both the direct effect of treatment on outcomes and the indirect effect arising from distortions in the running variable when treatment becomes available. Our identification strategy combines a conditional parallel trend assumption to recover untreated potential outcomes with a local invariance assumption that characterizes how the running variable responds to counterfactual policy cutoffs. These components allow us to identify and estimate counterfactual treatment effects for any proposed threshold.

Finally, we apply our framework to the Italian Domestic Stability Pact, where population-based fiscal rules generate both behavioral responses and running-variable distortions.

keenable.title: Causal inference in staggered adoption panels: The correct comparison set depends on your intervention
keenable.snippet:
A powerful data structure for causal inference is staggered adoption: many units are observed
over many time periods, during which some units adopt an irreversible treatment at various
time points while others remain untreated. Popular methods that apply in this setting include
difference in difference, fixed effects, matching, and synthetic control. All of these methods
compare the future outcomes of treatment adopters and non-adopters to answer the question:
for units who adopt treatment, what outcomes would have been realized if they had remained
untreated? We show that this question actually hides two very different causal questions of
interest. The first is what would have happened under a momentary intervention to prevent
treatment at its factual adoption time. The second is what would have happened to a treated
unit under a longitudinal ban preventing treatment at all periods until outcome measurement.
We show how to answer each question under conditionally ignorable treatment adoption or
under parallel trends. We highlight that common methods cannot answer the second question
because this question requires a time-varying comparison set with time-varying weights.

keenable.title: Lee Bounds with a Continuous Treatment in Sample Selection
keenable.snippet: Sample selection bias arises in causal inference when a treatment affects both outcomes and researchers’ ability to observe them. We generalize Lee (2009)’s bounds for the average treatment effect of a binary treatment to a continuous/multivalued treatment. We bound the effect of lottery prize on earnings that are only observed for the employed and survey respondents. To identify the effect of always-takers who are selected into samples with observed outcomes regardless of their treatment values, we assume that if a subject is selected at some sufficient treatment values, then it remains selected at any other values. This novel sufficient treatment values assumption includes monotone treatment effect on selection as a special case. keenable.title: Exchangeable Gaussian Processes for Staggered-Adoption Policy Evaluation
keenable.snippet: We study the use of exchangeable multi-task Gaussian processes (GPs) for causal inference in panel data, applying the framework to two settings: one with a single treated unit subject to a once-and-for-all treatment and another with multiple treated units and staggered treatment adoption. ## Randomized Controlled Trials: Building the Counterfactual by Lottery  
An RCT estimates a policy effect by assigning subjects to treatment or control by lottery, so the control group shows what the treated group would have experienced without the treatment. Random assignment makes the two groups comparable in expectation on every characteristic, observed and unobserved, which means any difference in average outcomes after the intervention can be attributed to the treatment itself. The estimand is the average treatment effect (ATE), the difference in mean outcomes between the two groups. Instrumental variables enhance natural experiments by introducing exogenous variation that affects treatment uptake independently of confounding factors, allowing researchers to identify causal relationships where direct randomization is impossible. ## 5. Why is this research important?  
The paper warns researchers not to follow a simple rule such as “always include controls” or “always remove controls affected by treatment.”  
Instead, researchers should ask:  
- Was the variable measured before or after treatment?
- Could the treatment have changed it?

#### Learn More  
External validity in natural experiments is constrained because causal identification typically hinges on the local average treatment effect (LATE) for compliers—those individuals whose treatment status changes precisely due to the exogenous variation exploited in the study. This means the estimated effects may not generalize beyond this specific subgroup or the particular context of the natural shock, such as a policy discontinuity or lottery assignment, limiting applicability to the broader population or alternative settings where the same variation does not induce compliance. linkup.snippet:
### When Can Policy Timing Support Causal Identification?  
Policy implementation timing may create useful comparisons across periods or populations.  
For example, a government may introduce a digital assessment policy in some jurisdictions before others. If implementation timing is sufficiently unrelated to anticipated changes in outcomes, later-adopting jurisdictions may provide information about what would have happened to earlier adopters without the policy.  
However, timing is frequently endogenous. Institutions may adopt interventions earlier because they have greater readiness, more severe problems, or stronger expectations of improvement.  
Researchers should investigate whether adoption timing is associated with outcome trends and whether the chosen estimator accommodates staggered implementation and heterogeneous treatment effects.  
When difference-in-differences is used, the relevant [counterfactual trends assumption](https://manuelgarcia.info/guides/research/guide/parallel-trends-assumption-difference-in-differences) must be defended.  
An implementation schedule is therefore potentially informative, but not automatically exogenous.
### Which Analytical Strategy Should Be Used?  
The analytical strategy should correspond to the mechanism generating exposure variation.  
| Exposure pattern | Potential strategy | Key identification concern |
|---|---|---|
| Eligibility changes at a threshold | Regression discontinuity | Continuity and assignment integrity near the cutoff |
| Policy affects selected populations over time | Difference-in-differences | Credible untreated outcome trends |
| External factor changes treatment uptake | Instrumental variables | Relevance, independence, exclusion, and estimand-specific assumptions |
| System-wide intervention begins at a defined time | Interrupted time series | Counterfactual trajectory and concurrent events |
| One treated unit has several potential untreated comparators | Synthetic control or related methods |

linkup.snippet:
Is not the reason for a policy to change a trend? If there are no trends in need of changing, what use is policy? Sure, arguing about the trend implications of policy might be hard and rife with many of the sociological facts that you often note. But even so, without trend implications, what use is policy? Another way of putting it might be that trend measurement is a way of making policy beliefs pay rent. Of course folks might enforce that rent payment badly, or with biases, or for status gains, but there is still a kernel of purpose behind it.
Another point you mention is that policies are changed rarely and so we should not expect trends to be much affected by policy changes, at least not after controlling for many other trend changers. But there is something normative in your use of "rarely." One might say that while the number of policy changes that have had suitably large trend impacts is low, the trend impact of the few trend-impacting policy changes was extremely high. I am not making such a claim but I could envision folks making such a claim with regard to e.g. civil rights, gender wage gap, measure of freedom for affected minorities, etc. If someone derived utils from the improvement in the trends of these topics, and the degree to which they derived utils was super huge, then even that small amount of trend-changing policy would have been vastly worth all the cost of noisy, unproductive trend measurement and trend debate on a host of many other less possibly efficacious policies.
Another way of reading your post is that people simply have lottery-like preferences when it comes to how they attach utils to policy-induced trend changes. Spend lots of small costs analyzing many trends; always analyze policy in terms of the trends it might impact (even if there is weak evidence that it can actually impact the trend); and for the few lightning-strike policies that really do change trends dramatically this way, celebrate them lots; and for the others, oh well.

octen.title: Causal inference in staggered adoption panels: The correct comparison set depends on your intervention
octen.snippet:
Much of the recent econometric literature has emphasized that two-way fixed effects estimators can fail to recover interpretable average effects when treatment effects are heterogeneous ([Imai and Kim, 2021](#bib.bib17); [De Chaisemartin and d’Haultfoeuille, 2020](#bib.bib16)). This literature has developed alternative estimators based on difference-in-differences ([Callaway and Sant’Anna, 2021](#bib.bib18)), synthetic control ([Ben-Michael et al., 2022](#bib.bib30)), and combinations of the two ([Arkhangelsky et al., 2021](#bib.bib24)). We address a different question: which counterfactual do these comparisons identify, and when are their identifying assumptions justified? First, we distinguish the outcome under momentary prevention of adoption from the outcome under a longitudinal treatment ban. Second, we show how dynamic confounding threatens identification: treatment affects subsequent covariates or outcomes, which in turn influence both later treatment adoption and future outcomes. In this setting, restricting the comparison group to never-adopters, or dropping controls as they adopt without adjusting for their selective exit, can consequently bias estimates of the longitudinal counterfactual. We demonstrate that parallel pre-treatment trends do not rule out this bias. We establish identification results under both conditional ignorability and parallel trends assumptions, showing how the comparison sets and adjustments required to account for dynamic confounding depend on the intervention of interest and the identifying assumptions.

The two estimands at the core of our paper appear in some past work.

View PDF HTML (experimental)Abstract:Under interference, the treatment of some units affects the outcomes of others, so that the effect on a treated unit consists of a direct and a spillover component. A non-treated comparison group then generally identifies neither component, but the difference between the total effect on the treated and the spillover effect on the comparison units. We show that both components are identified separately when multiple pre-treatment periods are available, without an uncontaminated comparison group. Under no anticipation, pre-treatment outcomes are free of both components for every unit. Extrapolating the pre-treatment trend within a group, as in interrupted time series approaches, therefore identifies the counterfactual outcome in the absence of any treatment. Applied to the treated it gives the total effect on them, applied to the non-treated at a given level of exposure the spillover effect on them. Disentangling the two components in addition requires effect homogeneity across treated and non-treated units with the same exposure and covariates, as well as common support in exposure. We derive doubly robust and Neyman-orthogonal expressions for the effects of interest, which permits controlling for covariates by machine learning, and establish asymptotic normality. A simulation study confirms the root-$n$ behaviour of the estimators and the reliability of the standard errors.

Overcoming vaccine hesitancy is critical to containing the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States. To increase vaccination rates, the State of Ohio launched a million dollar lottery in May 2021. Throughout, the decision-maker controls an encouragement or recommendation, not treatment uptake itself. Our analysis relies on a covariate-conditional exclusion restriction/assumption of no direct effect of encouragement on outcomes. Conditional on observed covariates, encouragement affects outcomes only through its effect on treatment take-up. This assumption encodes the “nudge” nature of encouragements, and it enables us to conceptually separate the effects of nudges on treatment take-up from the effects of treatments on downstream outcomes. To interpret that decomposition in terms of heterogeneous treatment effects, we additionally invoke treatment unconfoundedness; under truly randomized encouragement, alternative IV-style interpretations are also available. We therefore study policies that choose who to encourage so as to maximize policy value under the induced treatment behavior, optionally subject to budget and fairness constraints on induced treatment take-up or other groupwise impacts.
Optimal personalized policies often are optimizing in the space of encouragements, not treatments. Marginal encouragement effects are often enough for operational decision-making. For example, revenue management and pricing maximizes the expected profit, corresponding to the intention-to-treat effect. Operational goals to make better decisions differ from scientific goals to estimate the specific causal effect of receiving treatment, which gives rise to more challenging instrumental variables estimands.

## Chapter 4: Instrumental Variables and the LATE Theorem

Chapter 3 ended in a corner. When selection runs on something you cannot measure, ability in the schooling problem, no set of controls identifies the causal effect, and piling on covariates can make things worse. So we need a different idea entirely. Instead of trying to *adjust away* the confounding, we go looking for a source of variation in the treatment that is *itself* as-good-as-random, a lever that pushes people into or out of treatment for reasons unrelated to their potential outcomes. If we can find such a lever, we can trace its effect on the outcome and back out the effect of the treatment, sidestepping the unobserved confounder without ever measuring it.

That lever is an **instrumental variable**, and it is one of the most powerful and most misunderstood tools in econometrics. Powerful, because it can identify a causal effect even when confounders are unobserved. Misunderstood, because what it identifies is usually *not* the effect you first had in mind. IV forces the sharpest confrontation yet with **Thread B**, "what exactly did we identify?", and its honest answer, delivered by the LATE theorem, is that IV recovers the effect on a specific and often invisible subpopulation: the *compliers*. Every design in this book is an argument that this term is zero. There is one argument so clean it feels like cheating: *decide who gets treated by flipping a coin*. If a coin, and nothing about the person, determines DiD_i, then the treated and untreated groups cannot differ systematically in anything, including their untreated potential outcomes. This is why the randomized controlled trial (RCT) is the benchmark against which every observational design is measured. When economists call a natural experiment "credible," what they mean is "it approximates what a randomized experiment would have done." So we need to understand exactly *why* randomization works, and then, with equal seriousness, exactly what it still cannot deliver. A chapter that only sang the praises of RCTs would be teaching you half the craft and setting you up to overtrust a clean-looking experiment. ## Chapter 22: Causal Inference

We've spent 21 chapters learning to measure, estimate, test, and predict. But there's one question we've repeatedly deferred: **why?**

Statistical association tells you that ice cream sales and drowning rates move together. Statistical tests tell you this correlation is significant. Regression confirms the association holds after controlling for several covariates. But does eating ice cream cause drowning? Obviously not — hot weather drives both.

Causal inference is the formal machinery for moving from association to causation. It's not just a philosophical nicety. Every important question in medicine, economics, and policy is causal: Does this drug cure the disease? Does college education increase earnings? Does the minimum wage reduce employment? These cannot be answered by correlation or regression alone.

---

## 22.1 The Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference

### The Potential Outcomes Framework

The modern approach to causation, developed by Donald Rubin, uses **potential outcomes** (also called counterfactuals).

### Definition: Potential Outcomes

For each unit ii, define:

- Yi(1)Y_i(1): the outcome if unit ii receives treatment
- Yi(0)Y_i(0): the outcome if unit ii receives control

The **individual treatment effect** for unit ii is:

τi=Yi(1)−Yi(0)\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)

The **average treatment effect (ATE)** is:

τ=E[Y(1)−Y(0)]=E[Y(1)]−E[Y(0)]\tau = E[Y(1) - Y(0)] = E[Y(1)] - E[Y(0)]

**The fundamental problem:** We can only observe one of Yi(1)Y_i(1) or Yi(0)Y_i(0) for each unit. If patient ii receives the drug, we see Yi(1)Y_i(1) but never Yi(0)Y_i(0) (the counterfactual outcome if they hadn't received it).

**Example:** A patient with high blood pressure takes a medication and their blood pressure drops from 160 to 130 mmHg. Did the medication cause the drop?

We observe Yi(1)=130Y_i(1) = 130 (on medication).

## Why This Matters

Most policy questions cannot be answered by a randomized trial. A minimum-wage change, a school reform, a tariff, a tax credit: the intervention is allocated by legislatures, geography, or eligibility cutoffs, and the analyst sees one realization. The credibility revolution (Angrist and Pischke 2010) reorganized empirical economics around research designs that recover causal effects under transparent, testable assumptions rather than around structural models that require many more.

Three identification results carry most of the load: difference-in-differences (DiD) under parallel trends, regression discontinuity (RDD) under continuity at the cutoff, and instrumental variables (IV) under exogeneity and monotonicity. #### A rollout can create useful evidence even when you cannot randomize users. The comparison still has to earn a causal interpretation.

Your team introduces a new onboarding process in one market because its support team is ready first. Activation improves. That is encouraging, but the market also received a new acquisition campaign. A before-and-after chart cannot tell you how much improvement came from onboarding, the campaign, or changes that would have happened anyway.

A **quasi-experiment** uses a nonrandom assignment process and an explicit comparison strategy to estimate an intervention's effect. The comparison might come from another market, an eligibility cutoff, a policy rule, or a carefully modeled historical pattern. Its credibility depends on why that comparison represents what would have happened without the intervention.

This guide organizes the main designs around those opportunities. You'll learn which rollout situations support each design, what effects they can estimate, and which assumptions remain vulnerable even when a result looks statistically precise.

###### Abstract

I study fuzzy difference-in-differences designs from a design-based perspective, in which potential outcomes and treatment decisions are fixed and only the assignment of a policy is random, with heterogeneous and possibly unknown assignment probabilities. The Wald-DiD design estimand equals an assignment-weighted complier effect plus contamination from switchers, from changes in always-takers’ effects and from trends in untreated outcomes. ultimate.title: Evaluating Threshold Policies in Randomized Threshold Designs: A Cautionary Tale for Regression Discontinuity Designs
ultimate.snippet: Many policies assign treatment according to whether a score crosses a cutoff. Regression discontinuity (RD) designs identify the effect of treatment assignment, but the threshold policy itself may also reshape individuals’ incentives, inducing behavioral responses that affect outcomes even holding treatment status fixed—a channel that conventional RD designs cannot capture. We develop a framework that exploits randomized variation in policy thresholds, together with rank-invariance-type restrictions, to identify the treatment-assignment and incentive-response effects. We illustrate the empirical relevance of this distinction using data from a merit-based scholarship experiment in Malawi. In this illustration, the conventional RD estimate is positive, while the incentive-response effect is negative and more than twice as large in magnitude. These findings suggest that threshold policies may generate unintended adverse behavioral responses, potentially reflecting discouragement induced by demanding thresholds, and caution against relying solely on conventional RD estimates when evaluating threshold policies.

ultimate.title: Treatment Effects in the Regression Discontinuity Model with Counterfactual Cutoff and Distorted Running Variables
ultimate.snippet:
We develop a new framework for evaluating the total policy effect in regression discontinuity designs (RDD), incorporating both the direct effect of treatment on outcomes and the indirect effect arising from distortions in the running variable when treatment becomes available. Our identification strategy combines a conditional parallel trend assumption to recover untreated potential outcomes with a local invariance assumption that characterizes how the running variable responds to counterfactual policy cutoffs. These components allow us to identify and estimate counterfactual treatment effects for any proposed threshold.

Finally, we apply our framework to the Italian Domestic Stability Pact, where population-based fiscal rules generate both behavioral responses and running-variable distortions.

ultimate.title: Causal inference in staggered adoption panels: The correct comparison set depends on your intervention
ultimate.snippet:
A powerful data structure for causal inference is staggered adoption: many units are observed
over many time periods, during which some units adopt an irreversible treatment at various
time points while others remain untreated. Popular methods that apply in this setting include
difference in difference, fixed effects, matching, and synthetic control. All of these methods
compare the future outcomes of treatment adopters and non-adopters to answer the question:
for units who adopt treatment, what outcomes would have been realized if they had remained
untreated? We show that this question actually hides two very different causal questions of
interest. The first is what would have happened under a momentary intervention to prevent
treatment at its factual adoption time. The second is what would have happened to a treated
unit under a longitudinal ban preventing treatment at all periods until outcome measurement.
We show how to answer each question under conditionally ignorable treatment adoption or
under parallel trends. We highlight that common methods cannot answer the second question
because this question requires a time-varying comparison set with time-varying weights.

To make progress on narrowing the potential pathways, we survey two samples—city employees responding for 25 trials that did not adopt a nudge treatment after finding positive effects, and 45 city policymakers not involved in the trials.
We define adoption as the case in which “one nudge treatment arm has been used in communications from the city department after the RCT”. Given that the nudge arm was never the status-quo communication, adoption corresponds to a policy change. In the large majority of cases, whether a nudge treatment arm was adopted was straightforward to code. For the example in Figure A.1, the most recent communication (Figure A.1c) is clearly based on the nudge treatment letter (Figure A.1b), and is thus a case of adoption. In other cases, the recent communication resembles the communication in the control group, or there is simply no communication sent out in the years following the RCT; we code these cases as instances of non-adoption.
